content:
Christians often describe the first followers of Jesus as one community with one message. Paul's own letter to the Galatians records something else: a public quarrel at Antioch in which he accused Peter, the leading disciple of Jesus, of hypocrisy to his face.

"But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned" (Galatians 2:11).[1] Peter had walked with Jesus; Paul had not. The account is Paul's alone, and Peter's reply is not recorded anywhere.

This article aims to provide context to the quarrel, insha'Allah, in five facts from Galatians and Acts, each read for what it shows and what it does not. The Quran honours the disciples who answered Jesus: "We are Allah's helpers: We believe in Allah, and do thou bear witness that we are Muslims" (3:52).[2]

Paul tells the Galatians that he confronted Peter "before them all" (Galatians 2:14).[1] Peter, called Cephas in Paul's letters, was the first of the Twelve. Paul had joined the movement years after Jesus had gone, on the strength of a vision.

Christians read the scene as an apostle correcting another apostle's lapse. It is also a record of how authority was argued among the first believers: a man whose claim rested on revelation set it against a man whose claim rested on having been with Jesus. We set out how Paul's claim was received in Paul's claim to apostleship.

"For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision" (Galatians 2:12).[1]

Shared meals were where the question of the Law met daily life. Jewish believers kept the food laws; Gentile believers did not. Whether the two could eat together, and on whose terms, decided whether they were one community. Paul's charge to Peter puts the issue in a sentence: "If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?" (Galatians 2:14).[1]

The men who changed Peter's mind came "from James", the brother of Jesus and the leader of the believers in Jerusalem. Paul names James, Cephas and John as those "who were reputed to be pillars" (Galatians 2:9).[1]

Galatians does not say whether James sent them with instructions or whether they only came from his circle. Acts, written later, presents James at the Jerusalem council proposing that Gentile believers "abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood" (Acts 15:20).[3] How that council relates in time to the quarrel at Antioch is still argued. What both sources show is that James held the Law in a way that Paul's mission tested. We set out the Jerusalem decree in food offered to idols.

"And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy; so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy" (Galatians 2:13).[1] Barnabas was the man who had vouched for Paul in Jerusalem when the disciples "were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple" (Acts 9:26 to 27).[3]

At Antioch, Paul's closest companion took the other side. Acts later records that Paul and Barnabas parted over John Mark: "the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39).[3] Acts gives the cause as Mark, so the two quarrels should be kept apart. Together they show that Paul's nearest allies did not always stand with him. Apostle of Doom follows the three men through both quarrels in Paul, Barnabas and Peter.

Galatians ends the scene with Paul's speech and goes on to his argument about faith and the Law. It does not say whether Peter accepted the rebuke, whether Barnabas returned to Paul, or whether James answered. Acts does not mention the quarrel at all.

The only account is Paul's, written to defend his own authority against teachers who disputed it. An earlier agreement shows the two men had divided the work: Peter "with the Good News for the circumcised", Paul with it "for the uncircumcised" (Galatians 2:7).[1] How the quarrel ended, the record does not say.

The bottom line

At Antioch, Paul publicly accused Peter of hypocrisy for withdrawing from meals with Gentile believers when men came from James, and Barnabas sided with Peter. The account is Paul's own, written to defend his authority, and no source gives Peter's reply or the outcome.

The scene shows that within a generation of Jesus his followers disagreed openly about what his message required, and that the man whose letters would shape Christianity stood against Peter, the first of the disciples who had known Jesus. The Quran calls those disciples "Allah's helpers" (61:14), and asks every later claimant to be measured by the message they received.[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Galatians 2:7 to 14 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 3:52; 61:14, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Acts 9:26 to 27; 15:19 to 20; 15:36 to 40 (World English Bible).
